AM-T650 simulation comparison · Isaac at real time (RTF 1)

Whole-body L1 impedance vs geometric L1 adaptive vs modular adaptive control

Three controllers flew the same end-effector circle (radius 0.5 m, 24 s lap, the arm's second joint swinging 25 ± 15° on a 6 s period), and two of them then flew a faster figure-8 (1.5 × 0.75 m, 0.20 m/s mean end-effector speed, 3.4× the circle's peak yaw rate). All flights used one Isaac plant built from identified flight disturbances, one trajectory planner and one SAFETY takeoff/landing loop. The controllers are our whole-body L1 impedance law; the geometric controller with L1 adaptive augmentation of Cai et al. (CEP 2025); and the modular adaptive law of Yadav et al. (TMECH 2025). Only the DIRECT control law differed, plus, for the geometric law, how the arm is driven: its paper treats the arm separately, so the arm runs a position-mode stack tracking the planner's joint reference, where the other two command arm torques. All results are from Isaac running at real time (RTF 1). The whole-body law flew its shipped configuration, which was tuned on this plant's offline bench; the geometric and modular laws were implemented from their papers and tuned for this plant on the same bench with the same search. Section 1 gives the reference trajectories.

1. Reference trajectories

Both trajectories are generated by the same planner (fsc_trajectory_planner, end-effector trajectory mode) from a prescribed end-effector pose curve, an assigned arm sinusoid and one time law. The planner solves the rest for a dynamically compatible whole-body reference, and every controller in this report receives that same reference. The whole-body and modular laws take it directly. The geometric law takes the base position, velocity, acceleration and yaw that the reference bridge converts from it.

Time law (both shapes)
dτdt=sσ(u),u=min(1, min(t, T−t)Tr),σ(u)=35u4−84u5+70u6−20u7,T=2Tr+NTlap−sTrs

τ is the shape phase in seconds and t the time since Start. Each run starts and ends at rest: a minimum-snap ramp of Tr=4 s, then N laps at the constant rate s (the time scale), then the mirrored ramp-out. On the ramps σ rises from 0 to 1 with zero first three derivatives at both ends. All flights here use N=1 lap at s=1.

End-effector position: circle
pe(τ)=(rcos(θ0+ωτ), rsin(θ0+ωτ), he)⊤,ω=2πTlap,v¯=2πrTlap

Centred on the world vertical axis at the hold's end-effector height he. The run starts at the circle point on the hold's end-effector bearing θ0 and turns counter-clockwise.

End-effector position: figure-8
pe(τ)=pe0+Rz(ψ0−α)(Asinωτ, Bsin2ωτ, 0)⊤,α=atan2(2B,A),v¯=1Tlap∫02πA2cos2ϕ+4B2cos22ϕdϕ

The lobes cross at the hold's end-effector point pe0, where the run starts and ends. A is the half-length along the long axis and B the half-width across it. The start tangent lies along the drone's nose ψ0, so the long axis sits at ψ0−α (45° for B=A/2). The right lobe is flown clockwise and the left lobe counter-clockwise, so the yaw rate reverses at the crossing. The mean speed v¯ is the path length of one lap over Tlap, as the arm ground station computes it.

End-effector attitude: claw along the path
ψt(τ)=atan2(p˙e,y,p˙e,x),Re(τ)=Rz(ψt−π2)Rx(βe),b1e=Ree1=(sinψt, −cosψt, 0)⊤

The end-effector heading follows the path tangent ψt, with the fixed fold βe=55∘ about the horizontal axis b1e (the claw points along the direction of travel, 35–40° below the horizontal). b1e is the tracked end-effector heading, and its azimuth error is the "EE heading" column of the tables.

Arm: the assigned redundancy
q1=0,q2(τ)=q¯2+a2sin2πτP,P=Tlap4,(ψ, β, γ)=zxz(Rtilt(n)⊤Re),q3=β−q2,q4=γ

The base-yaw joint q1 is fixed and the shoulder q2 is the assigned sinusoid, four periods per lap on both shapes. The drone yaw ψ, the fold β=q2+q3 and the wrist roll γ=q4 are the z–x–z angles of the end-effector attitude seen from the tilted airframe, where Rtilt(n) is the minimal rotation taking e3 to the thrust direction n.

System centre of mass: the compatible flat output
xc=pe+R0(r0c(q)−r0e(q)),n=x¨c+ge3‖x¨c+ge3‖,R0=R0(n, ψ)

The thrust direction depends on the CoM acceleration, which depends on the attitude, so the planner solves this as a fixed point (Picard iteration). xc is fitted as a degree-7 B-spline, ψ and q as degree-5 B-splines. The streamed reference is their flat map: xcd and its derivatives to snap, the base heading, the end-effector position and heading, and qd, q˙d.

RMS over the EXECUTING window of each flight (one lap, 24 s of plan time). All nine circle flights ran under one condition: headless Isaac, the real-time pacer holding RTF 1.000, Isaac pinned to the performance cores from launch, the same plant and controller files. EE/base position and EE/base heading are tracking error against the planner's reference; joints are measured minus the streamed joint reference. All nine flights completed the lap without rotor saturation (the geometric law's motor commands stayed within 0.49–0.73); the whole-body and modular flights also had no joint-torque clamp. All nine started the lap through the planner's standard 0.10 m Start gate. The geometric law flew gains tuned for this plant (section 4.3). With its hardware flight configuration it scored 206 mm / 9.60° on the same mission (EE path 0.69–0.70 m), matching its hardware flights of 2026-09-28, and needed the Start gate widened to 0.25 m. The error that remains is structural to the paper's law. Its L1 augmentation acts only on the matched channel (thrust and body torque), so it estimates the body-fixed lateral force, (0.46, −0.45) N, but does not cancel it. The pure-P position loop therefore leaves the airframe F/Kp ≈ 0.74 N / 20.1 ≈ 37 mm off, turning with the heading (measured hover offset 38 mm). With ωd = 0 its attitude damping opposes the circle's 15°/s yaw rate, a (Kω/KR)·rate ≈ (0.41/1.74)·15°/s ≈ 3.5° heading lag that the position-mode arm carries to the gripper, so its EE heading error equals its base yaw error. The whole-body law's own q1/q4 carry the end-effector heading redundancy — it tracks the end effector, not a fixed joint split — so its small per-joint numbers are not directly comparable to the modular law's, which has no such redundancy to spend.

3. Figure-8: tracking performance comparison

Whole-body L1 (shipped)Geometric L1 adaptive (tuned)

The whole-body and geometric L1 laws then flew a faster figure-8 under the launch condition of section 2: headless Isaac, the real-time pacer holding RTF 1.000 in every 10 s window, Isaac pinned to the performance cores from launch, the same plant and controller files, and the geometric law on its tuned gains. The modular law was not flown on this shape. Each flight took off in SAFETY to 1.2 m at a 45° heading, switched to DIRECT, passed the same stability gate, flew to the run's start rest, then flew one lap at time scale 1.

3.1 Choosing the figure-8

The brief was a mean end-effector speed of about 0.20 m/s (the circle's is 0.131 m/s); a figure-8 "radius" of 0.60–0.75 m to fit the flight area, taken as the half-length A (the planner's counterpart of the circle radius, 0.5 m in earlier figure-8 runs); and the arm's q2 swinging on a period that divides the lap, four periods per lap as on the circle. The half-width is B = A/2, the planner's default proportion, which makes each lobe as wide as it is long. At a fixed mean speed a smaller 8 turns harder. The planner's own numbers for each candidate, at 0.20 m/s and time scale 1:

A [m]B [m]path [m]Tlap at 0.20 m/s [s]q2 period Tlap/4 [s]peak CoM speed [m/s]peak CoM accel. [m/s²]peak yaw rate [°/s]smax (binding bound)
0.600.3003.65818.294.5730.3290.46564.60.89 (CoM speed)

0.750.3004.13920.695.1740.2750.31048.01.08 (CoM speed)
0.750.2253.74418.724.6800.2660.29645.11.12 (CoM speed)

Where the path turns fastest (the top and bottom of each lobe) the airframe swings around the end effector, so the CoM speed peaks above the end effector's 0.29 m/s. The planner's CoM speed bound of 0.30 m/s therefore rules out A = 0.60 and 0.65 m at this speed (smax below 1). A = 0.75 m is the largest size in the range and has the most margin (smax 1.07), with the lowest yaw rate and CoM acceleration. A thinner 8 (B = 0.30 or 0.225 m) would lower the peak yaw rate by only 6–12 %. Chosen: A = 0.75 m, B = 0.375 m, Tlap = 22.865 s (0.200 m/s mean), q2 = 25 ± 15° on a 5.716 s period, fold 55°, the circle's arm amplitude, centre and fold.

The planner's shared bounds (CoM acceleration 0.15 m/s², yaw rate 0.30 rad/s) would cap this shape at s = 0.34, i.e. 0.068 m/s. Those bounds also size every transition (go-to-start, back-to-origin, ground-station targets). Rather than raise them, the planner gained bounds for the end-effector run only: ee_traj_a_max = 0.40 m/s² and ee_traj_w_max = 1.0 rad/s (0 = inherit, so every other mode is unchanged). With them smax = 1.06, set by the shared 0.30 m/s CoM speed, and every flight below ran at s = 1.00.

Whole-body L1. The end-effector error rises from 15.0 mm on the circle to 23.5 mm, and the rise sits where the yaw rate is high: 28.6 mm RMS where |ψ̇| exceeds 35°/s against 19.4 mm where it is below 20°/s. The heading error stays at 0.78° RMS (peak 1.9°), and its dependence on the yaw rate is weak (0.023 s), because the law receives the full reference chain, yaw rate and acceleration included, and feeds it forward. Most of its end-effector error is airframe position (22.1 mm of the split); the attitude and joint terms grow only from 5.0 / 5.2 mm on the circle to 8.5 / 7.8 mm.

Geometric L1 adaptive. The heading error grows from 2.97° to 6.84° RMS (peak 15.9°), and it is almost entirely the constant-yaw specialization's lag. A least-squares fit of the end-effector heading error on the reference yaw rate gives −0.257 s (R² 0.95), against the predicted Kω,z/KR,z = 0.411/1.737 = 0.237 s for ωd = 0; on the circle the same fit gives −0.251 s. At the figure-8's 51°/s that lag is 12–15°, and the position-mode arm carries it to the gripper. Through the arm's 0.23–0.28 m horizontal reach the same lag also moves the end-effector position: the airframe-attitude term of the split doubles from 15.9 mm on the circle to 31.8 mm, about reach × heading error (0.25 m × 6.84° ≈ 30 mm). The end-effector position error rises from 48.9 to 59.5 mm, concentrated at the high yaw rates (78.1 against 48.4 mm).

The rest of the geometric law's error is the offset section 2 already showed. Its L1 augmentation estimates the body-fixed lateral force (+0.55, −0.50) N but cannot cancel it, so the pure-P position loop parks the airframe F/Kp = (+27, −25) mm off in the body frame (37 mm before Start). Because the nose follows the path tangent, the body frame is the path frame, and the end effector rides 30 mm ahead of and 28 mm to the right of its reference on average. On the circle the same offset showed as a wider, leading circle; on the figure-8 it shifts each lobe differently, since the right lobe turns clockwise and the left counter-clockwise.

On the circle the whole-body law tracked the end effector 3.3× better than the geometric law in position and 5.9× in heading; on the figure-8 the margins are 2.5× and 8.8×.

4. Simulation settings

4.1 Uncertainties, rotor motor delay and robustness injections

The Isaac plant carries the disturbances identified from three real T650 indoor flights (2026‑09‑18/21/24) rather than an idealised model — all three controllers fly the identical injected plant below. The modular and geometric configuration files are generated from the whole-body one and checked against it key by key: the same plant, allocator beliefs, SAFETY loop and guards.

Arm drive. The whole-body and modular laws command joint torques. The geometric law's arm is position-commanded, as in its paper; Isaac emulates the position servo as PD (3.0 N·m/rad, 0.25 N·m·s/rad) plus an integral term (2.0 N·m/(rad·s), clamped at 0.35 N·m) plus gravity compensation, through the same servo model. So the gearbox-friction and current-noise injections reach all three arms. The joint-velocity feedback lag matters only to the two laws that read joint velocity.

Geometric L1 adaptive law (Cai et al.)

A geometric SE(3) controller (position loop plus attitude error on SO(3)) with the arm's centre-of-mass offset ros compensated live from the arm encoders, augmented by an L1 adaptive term on the matched channel (thrust and body torque). The gains below were tuned for this plant (section 4.3); its hardware flight configuration of 2026-09-28 is given in brackets. Model terms, limits and the arm compensation are as flown. Our implementation runs the paper's constant-position/constant-yaw specialization, because the position reference it receives carries no yaw-rate field: the desired angular velocity ωd = 0, so the circle's turning yaw reference enters only through the attitude error. The planner's whole-body reference is converted to a base position/velocity/acceleration/yaw reference for it by the reference bridge, with the planner's own base CoM.

4.3 How the geometric law was tuned

The geometric law was tuned the way the modular law was, on the same offline bench the whole-body tune came from. The bench runs an exact Python port of the C++ node (geometric law, L1 augmentation, ros from the encoders), the reference bridge and Isaac's position-mode arm servo, flying the comparison circle against the mirror plant with hardware-like feedback noise and lag. CMA-ES searched all 11 gains: Kp, Kv, KR and Kω for the horizontal and vertical axes, the two predictor poles and ωc. Each candidate flew the circle at the nominal 16 ms transport delay, at a longer delay it had to survive, and on the stress plant (mass and inertia × 1.10, arm mass and gearbox friction × 1.05, CoM shifted 10/10/5 mm, allocator thrust belief +17.6 %).

geometric gain setbench EE / heading, 3 noise seedssurvives delay up tostress plant EEIsaac at RTF 1
hardware configuration (2026-09-28)241 mm / 10.3°44 ms (aborts at 60)aborts206 mm / 9.60°, 3 of 3 completed
stage 1: must survive 28 ms43 mm / 2.0°28 ms (aborts at 30)53 mmdiverged before the lap, 1 of 1
stage 2: must survive 44 ms (flown above)58 mm / 3.4°52 ms (highest tested)70 mm48.9 mm / 2.97°, 3 of 3 completed

Stage 1 used the 28 ms bar the other two laws meet on this bench: the whole-body tune survives 28 ms and aborts at 30, the modular tune survives 34 ms and aborts at 36. Its best set diverged in Isaac. A 1.53 Hz attitude oscillation grew from the switch into DIRECT until the vehicle passed 40° of tilt 19 s later, before the lap began. The bench reproduces that same mode at 30 ms of delay (and for the hardware set at 60 ms), so Isaac puts more effective delay around this law than 28 ms. Stage 2 therefore required 44 ms. The search met it mainly by lowering the L1 filter bandwidth ωc from 6 to 1 rad/s, which keeps the L1 torque correction out of the rotor-lag band near 1.5 Hz; the position and attitude gains stayed close to stage 1. At ωc = 1 rad/s the augmentation compensates disturbances slower than about 0.16 Hz and leaves faster ones to the geometric loop. The tuned set has not been flown on hardware.
